readings.title: On Liberty, II: the deep slumber of a decided opinion
readings.challenge: Follow Mill as he raises an objection against himself and decides how much to concede.
readings.focus: Why even settled truths need opponents, real or imagined.
readings.context: John Stuart Mill’s On Liberty (1859) defends freedom of thought and of individual life against the pressure of law and of public opinion. In Chapter II he has just argued that creeds inherited without discussion become dead formulas. Here he extends the point to proverbs and everyday wisdom. Pro and con means for and against; cram is memorized learning; “Socratici viri” means the men trained by Socrates; a dissentient is one who disagrees.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, “Of the Liberty of Thought and Discussion,” from “The same thing holds true” through the praise of those who contest a received opinion; opens “The same thing holds true, generally speaking, of all traditional doctrines—those of…”; closes “…or the vitality of our convictions, to do with much greater labour for ourselves.”.

questions.prompt: Why, according to Mill, do people often understand a familiar proverb only after a misfortune, and what else might have taught them sooner?
facilitatorNotes: Sayings are repeated as truisms until painful experience makes them real. Mill grants that some truths need experience, but says much more would be understood if people had heard them argued for and against by those who understood them.
evidence: of which most people first truly learn the meaning, when experience, generally of a painful kind, has made it a reality to them
if the man had been accustomed to hear it argued pro and con. by people who did understand it

questions.prompt: What objection does Mill raise against himself in his string of questions, and how much does he concede?
facilitatorNotes: If truth needs disagreement, must some people stay in error, and does agreement destroy a truth? He denies this: growing agreement on true opinions is a mark of progress. But losing the need to defend a truth is “no trifling drawback,” so teachers should invent a substitute for a real opponent.
evidence: Do the fruits of conquest perish by the very completeness of the victory?
though not sufficient to outweigh, is no trifling drawback from, the benefit of its universal recognition

questions.prompt: Why does Mill value “negative logic,” and what does he find missing from modern education?
facilitatorNotes: Socratic questioning showed people that they did not understand the commonplaces they professed, and medieval disputation made pupils state both sides. Negative criticism is a poor end but an indispensable means to real conviction. Modern instruction from teachers and books compels no one to hear the other side.
evidence: Such negative criticism would indeed be poor enough as an ultimate result; but as a means to attaining any positive knowledge or conviction worthy the name, it cannot be valued too highly
the weakest part of what everybody says in defence of his opinion, is what he intends as a reply to antagonists

questions.prompt: Mill ends by asking us to thank those who contest received opinions. Is this gratitude reasonable even when the dissenter is wrong?
facilitatorNotes: On his argument, yes: the dissenter does the work of testing our convictions that we would otherwise have to do ourselves. Readers may raise limits, such as bad-faith or harmful dissent, and ask whether Mill’s argument depends on the dissenter arguing honestly.
evidence: let us thank them for it, open our minds to listen to them
what we otherwise ought, if we have any regard for either the certainty or the vitality of our convictions, to do with much greater labour for ourselves

readings.title: On Liberty, III: the despotism of custom
readings.challenge: Separate the structure of an argument from the historical generalizations offered as its evidence.
readings.focus: Uniformity as a threat to progress, even in a society that prides itself on change.
readings.context: John Stuart Mill’s On Liberty (1859) defends freedom of thought and of individual life against the pressure of law and of public opinion. In Chapter III he argues that individuality is part of human well-being, and has just complained that public opinion in his England discourages any marked difference. To proscribe is to forbid; a régime is a system of rule. Alexis de Tocqueville was a French writer on democracy, and Wilhelm von Humboldt a German thinker Mill quoted earlier.
readings.contentNote: Mill claims that “the whole East” has no history and holds up China as a nation that became stationary. These are nineteenth-century European generalizations, open to historical challenge.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, “Of Individuality, as One of the Elements of Well-being,” the two paragraphs beginning “The despotism of custom” and “What is it that has hitherto preserved Europe”; opens “The despotism of custom is everywhere the standing hindrance to human advancement, being…”; closes “…taking under its protection opinions and tendencies at variance with those of the public.”.

questions.prompt: How does Mill distinguish the spirit of improvement from the spirit of liberty, and why does he call liberty the only permanent source of improvement?
facilitatorNotes: Improvement can be forced on an unwilling people, and liberty may resist it. Liberty is the lasting source because it creates as many independent centres of improvement as there are individuals: progress depends on many different experiments, not one reformer’s plan.
evidence: for it may aim at forcing improvements on an unwilling people
there are as many possible independent centres of improvement as there are individuals

questions.prompt: What kind of “despotism of custom” threatens Europe, according to Mill, and how does fashion illustrate it?
facilitatorNotes: Not standing still but changing together: it forbids singularity while allowing change, as long as everyone changes at once. Everyone dresses like everyone else, though the fashion shifts; change happens for its own sake rather than from anyone’s own idea of beauty or use.
evidence: It proscribes singularity, but it does not preclude change, provided all change together.
It is individuality that we war against

questions.prompt: How does Mill use China as evidence, and where is that evidence weakest?
facilitatorNotes: China had excellent customs and an educational system that put the wisest in power, yet, he claims, became stationary for thousands of years. The argument’s structure is that uniform excellence still stops progress. But the historical claims, especially that the whole East has “no history,” are sweeping, unsupported generalizations; students can accept or reject the structure separately from the example.
evidence: The greater part of the world has, properly speaking, no history, because the despotism of Custom is complete.
We have a warning example in China

questions.prompt: Which forces does Mill say are making people alike, and why is it striking that he lists them?
facilitatorNotes: Political changes that raise the low and lower the high, wider education, better communication, commerce, and above all the rule of public opinion. Many are reforms Mill elsewhere welcomes. He does not oppose them; he warns that as differences of situation shrink, no social power remains to protect nonconformity.
evidence: Every extension of education promotes it
there ceases to be any social support for nonconformity

readings.title: On Liberty, I: the tyranny of opinion
readings.challenge: List the forces Mill says have made a society’s moral rules, and ask which of them are reasons.
readings.focus: Why the pressure of opinion can be harder to escape than the pressure of law.
readings.context: John Stuart Mill’s On Liberty (1859) defends freedom of thought and of individual life against the pressure of law and of public opinion. Earlier in Chapter I he traced how liberty once meant protection against rulers, and how elected government brought a new danger: the will of the majority imposed on the rest. Helots were the serfs of ancient Sparta and roturiers French commoners; odium theologicum is Latin for the hatred of theologians; a Unitarian is a Christian who rejects the Trinity.
readings.contentNote: Mill uses period terms: “negroes” for the enslaved Black people on plantations, in a list of moralities made by ruling classes, and “Papist,” a hostile name for Roman Catholics, in describing how far other people’s tolerance stops.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, “Introductory,” from “Like other tyrannies” through the limits of religious toleration; opens “Like other tyrannies, the tyranny of the majority was at first, and is still vulgarly,…”; closes “…still genuine and intense, it is found to have abated little of its claim to be obeyed.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Mill think social tyranny can be “more formidable” than political oppression, though its penalties are usually milder?
facilitatorNotes: It leaves fewer means of escape and reaches into the details of life and into the soul, imposing ideas and practices by means other than law and fettering individuality. A prison sentence ends at the prison wall; disapproval follows a person everywhere. Students may name modern forms, from neighbours to social media.
evidence: it practises a social tyranny more formidable than many kinds of political oppression,
it leaves fewer means of escape, penetrating much more deeply into the details of life, and enslaving the soul itself.

questions.prompt: According to Mill, what usually guides people’s rules for other people’s conduct? Why does a preference shared by many remain “only many people’s liking”?
facilitatorNotes: Each person feels that everyone should act as he and those he sympathizes with would like. An opinion without reasons is a preference, and a reason that only appeals to the same preference in others adds numbers, not grounds. Mill is not saying all morality is preference, only that unreasoned rules are.
evidence: is the feeling in each person’s mind that everybody should be required to act as he, and those with whom he sympathizes, would like them to act.
it is still only many people’s liking instead of one.

questions.prompt: Mill names class interest and servility to masters or gods as sources of moral rules. Why does he insist that servility “is not hypocrisy,” and why does that make it more dangerous?
facilitatorNotes: The feelings it produces are genuine: people really do abhor what their masters or gods are thought to hate. Sincerity is what made men burn magicians and heretics. A defensible answer: hypocrisy can be exposed, but sincere feeling looks to its holders like conscience. Others will stress class interest, which Mill shows turning into the class’s own moral feelings.
evidence: a large portion of the morality of the country emanates from its class interests,
This servility, though essentially selfish, is not hypocrisy;
it made men burn magicians and heretics.

questions.prompt: Religious belief is the one case where liberty was claimed on principle. How, by Mill’s account, was that liberty actually won, and what does this suggest about how rights get won?
facilitatorNotes: Not mainly by conviction: neither side could win, so minorities pleaded for permission to differ, and toleration took hold chiefly where indifference wanted peace. Even then it comes with “tacit reserves,” and each person draws the line somewhere. A rights claim can win by stalemate and fatigue rather than agreement, which leaves it fragile wherever feeling is still intense.
evidence: minorities, seeing that they had no chance of becoming majorities, were under the necessity of pleading to those whom they could not convert, for permission to differ.
except where religious indifference, which dislikes to have its peace disturbed by theological quarrels, has added its weight to the scale.
the duty of toleration is admitted with tacit reserves.

readings.title: On Liberty, II: Socrates and Marcus Aurelius
readings.challenge: Notice why Mill chooses the cases least favourable to his own side, and how he refuses to make the persecutors villains.
readings.focus: How sincere and good people come to persecute the best people and ideas of their time.
readings.context: John Stuart Mill’s On Liberty (1859) defends freedom of thought and of individual life against the pressure of law and of public opinion. Earlier in Chapter II he argued that all silencing of discussion assumes infallibility. Plato’s Apology records Socrates’ defence at his trial in Athens; ‘i maëstri di color che sanno’ adapts Dante’s Italian for Aristotle, ‘the master of those who know.’ Calvary is the place outside Jerusalem where Jesus was crucified. Marcus Aurelius, also called Antoninus, was a Stoic philosopher and Roman emperor of the second century; Constantine was the first Christian emperor. Dr. Samuel Johnson was an eighteenth-century English writer.
readings.contentNote: Mill discusses the trial of Jesus and the persecution of the early Christians, following the Gospel accounts. His point is that the persecutors were sincere, ordinary people: he says most who now condemn the high priest would have done the same had they been born Jews in his time, against the old habit of blaming the Jews for the crucifixion, a charge long used to justify persecuting them.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, from “In order more fully to illustrate” through Dr. Johnson’s defence of persecution; opens “In order more fully to illustrate the mischief of denying a hearing to opinions because…”; closes “…for religious intolerance, sufficiently remarkable not to be passed without notice.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Mill test his argument on belief in God and a future state, cases “least favourable” to him? What, he says, is and is not the assumption of infallibility?
facilitatorNotes: The hardest case gives the strongest argument; if freedom holds there, it holds anywhere. Feeling sure is not the fault; deciding for others without letting them hear the other side is. The more solemn the conviction, the more fatal the mistake, because those are the occasions history remembers with horror.
evidence: I choose, by preference, the cases which are least favourable to me
It is the undertaking to decide that question for others, without allowing them to hear what can be said on the contrary side.
this is the case of all others in which it is most fatal.

questions.prompt: Mill insists that Socrates’ judges and Jesus’ accusers were not bad men. Why does that matter more to his argument than if they had been wicked?
facilitatorNotes: If they were villains, we could think ourselves safe from their mistake. Because they were honest, respectable and pious, with more than the usual moral feeling of their time, the same mistake is open to us. Mill makes fallibility the lesson, not wickedness.
evidence: honestly found him guilty,
not worse than men commonly are, but rather the contrary;
would have acted precisely as he did.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct Marcus Aurelius’s reasons for persecuting Christianity as fairly as Mill does. Why does Mill call this “one of the most tragical facts in all history”?
facilitatorNotes: He believed society was held together by reverence for the old gods; the new religion aimed to dissolve those ties; its theology seemed incredible to him; so, from duty, he put it down. It is tragic because his virtue and wisdom led him to the error; the best ruler of his age is Mill’s strongest evidence that no one is safe from it.
evidence: it was held together and prevented from being worse, by belief and reverence of the received divinities.
under a solemn sense of duty, authorized the persecution of Christianity.
To my mind this is one of the most tragical facts in all history.

questions.prompt: Mill dares anyone who would punish opinions to claim to be “a wiser and better man than Marcus Aurelius.” Is this a fair test? What might a defender of some limits on speech reply?
facilitatorNotes: Every plea now made for punishing opinions was available to Marcus, so whoever punishes must believe himself wiser. Against punishing opinions as false or impious the test is strong. A reply might point to speech that harms others, such as incitement, which the test does not touch and which Mill himself allows may be punished. Others will say modern evidence and courts do better than one emperor; Mill would ask whether they make anyone infallible.
evidence: flatters himself that he is a wiser and better man than Marcus Aurelius
let him abstain from that assumption of the joint infallibility of himself and the multitude,

readings.title: On Liberty, II: four grounds and fair discussion
readings.challenge: Restate Mill’s four grounds in a sentence each before you read his answer to those who want discussion kept temperate.
readings.focus: Who gains when only “temperate” discussion is allowed.
readings.context: John Stuart Mill’s On Liberty (1859) defends freedom of thought and of individual life against the pressure of law and of public opinion. Chapter II, on the liberty of thought and discussion, has argued that a silenced opinion may be true, and that even a true opinion never challenged decays into a dead formula. Here Mill sums up the chapter. Invective is abusive speech; personality here means personal attack; a polemic is a controversialist; calumny is slander; vituperation is abuse; infidelity here means unbelief.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, from the summary of its four grounds through “the real morality of public discussion”; opens “We have now recognised the necessity to the mental well-being of mankind (on which all…”; closes “…extent observe it, and a still greater number who conscientiously strive towards it.”.

questions.prompt: Restate Mill’s four grounds in your own words. Which depend on the silenced opinion being true or partly true, and which hold even if it is entirely false?
facilitatorNotes: The first holds if the opinion may be true; the second if it holds part of the truth, since the prevailing view is rarely the whole of it. The third and fourth hold even when the received opinion is the whole truth: unchallenged, it is held as prejudice, and then its meaning fades into a formula. These last two are Mill’s most original claim: a false dissent still serves the truth.
evidence: To deny this is to assume our own infallibility.
it is only by the collision of adverse opinions that the remainder of the truth has any chance of being supplied.
the dogma becoming a mere formal profession, inefficacious for good, but cumbering the ground,

questions.prompt: Why does Mill think offence is a poor test of whether discussion is temperate? Why can the worst faults of argument rarely be punished?
facilitatorNotes: Offence is given whenever an attack is telling, so the test would penalize good arguments, and any hard-to-answer opponent with strong feeling looks intemperate. The real faults, such as suppressing facts or misrepresenting the other side, are so often committed in good faith that they can rarely be proved blameworthy, and law could not reach them at all.
evidence: this offence is given whenever the attack is telling and powerful,
appears to them, if he shows any strong feeling on the subject, an intemperate opponent.
is so continually done in perfect good faith,

questions.prompt: Why, according to Mill, does abuse used on the side of the prevailing opinion do more harm than abuse used against it?
facilitatorNotes: Restraint is demanded only of the minority, while the majority’s invective is praised as zeal. A minority must be studiously moderate or lose ground, and it cannot safely call its opponents bad and immoral men; the majority can, and that deters people from professing or even hearing other views. The unfair advantage goes almost wholly to received opinions.
evidence: it is only desired to restrain the employment of them against the prevailing opinion:
The worst offence of this kind which can be committed by a polemic, is to stigmatize those who hold the contrary opinion as bad and immoral men.
really does deter people from professing contrary opinions, and from listening to those who profess them.

questions.prompt: Mill says attacks on unbelief need more discouraging than attacks on religion, yet that law has no business with either. What, then, should restrain them, and what is “the real morality of public discussion”? Apply it to an argument you have seen.
facilitatorNotes: Opinion, not law, judging each case on its merits: blame for want of candour, malignity, bigotry or intolerance on either side, and honour for anyone who states opponents’ views fairly, exaggerating nothing and holding back nothing in their favour. The standard is demanding but symmetrical; students can test it on a recent debate and ask who met it.
evidence: there would be much more need to discourage offensive attacks on infidelity, than on religion.
It is, however, obvious that law and authority have no business with restraining either,
who has calmness to see and honesty to state what his opponents and their opinions really are,

readings.title: On Liberty, IV: the public in the wrong place
readings.challenge: Separate Mill’s arguments against interfering with self-regarding conduct, then rank them.
readings.focus: Why the public is likely to judge wrongly when it judges conduct that concerns only the agent.
readings.context: John Stuart Mill’s On Liberty (1859) defends freedom of thought and of individual life against the pressure of law and of public opinion. Earlier in Chapter IV he divided conduct into what concerns others and what he calls self-regarding, which affects only the agent, and has just granted that self-harm which breaks a definite duty, like a soldier drunk on duty, may be punished. Nonage is childhood; Charles II became king in 1660, after the Puritans had ruled England; parity is equality.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “Of the Limits to the Authority of Society over the Individual,” from “But with regard to the merely contingent” through the promise of examples; opens “But with regard to the merely contingent, or, as it may be called, constructive injury…”; closes “…liberty of the individual, is one of the most universal of all human propensities.”.

questions.prompt: What does Mill mean by “contingent” or “constructive” injury to society? Why does he think society can afford to bear it?
facilitatorNotes: Harm that breaks no specific duty and hurts no assignable person except the agent, such as making oneself less useful to society. Freedom is worth more than that loss, and society cannot demand benefits it does not claim a right to. Mill would rather people were punished for their own sake than under that pretence.
evidence: nor occasions perceptible hurt to any assignable individual except himself;
the inconvenience is one which society can afford to bear, for the sake of the greater good of human freedom.

questions.prompt: Society has had “absolute power” over people in childhood. How does Mill turn that fact into an argument against controlling adults?
facilitatorNotes: Society already has education, the authority of received opinion and the natural penalties of others’ contempt. If it lets people grow up unable to act on distant motives, the fault is its own. Coercion also defeats itself: vigorous characters rebel, as grossness followed the Puritans.
evidence: Society has had absolute power over them during all the early portion of their existence:
society has itself to blame for the consequences.
they will infallibly rebel against the yoke.

questions.prompt: Why does Mill call his next argument “the strongest of all”? What difference does he see between the public judging duties to others and judging self-regarding conduct?
facilitatorNotes: On duties to others the majority judges its own interests, so it is more often right than wrong. On self-regarding conduct, public opinion is at best some people’s view of what is good for other people, and often only their own preference, so it is as likely wrong as right.
evidence: the odds are that it interferes wrongly, and in the wrong place.
public opinion means, at the best, some people’s opinion of what is good or bad for other people;

questions.prompt: Is Mill right that there is “no parity” between a person’s feeling for his own opinion and another’s offence at his holding it? Test his comparison of the thief and the purse.
facilitatorNotes: The owner keeps what is his; the thief wants what is another’s; so the offended person wants control over what belongs to someone else. The comparison works only if a person’s taste is his own concern, which is what Mill is arguing, so critics may call it circular. Others will say offence can be a real harm; Mill would answer that it gives no right to control.
evidence: But there is no parity between the feeling of a person for his own opinion, and the feeling of another who is offended at his holding it;
And a person’s taste is as much his own peculiar concern as his opinion or his purse.

readings.title: On Liberty, V: free not to be free
readings.challenge: Find the one case in which Mill says freedom itself sets a limit on freedom, then test how far his reason reaches.
readings.focus: Contracts and promises, and the obligations they create to people outside them.
readings.context: John Stuart Mill’s On Liberty (1859) defends freedom of thought and of individual life against the pressure of law and of public opinion. In Chapter V Mill applies his principle, that people should be free in what concerns only themselves, to practical questions. Earlier in the essay he quoted Wilhelm von Humboldt, a German scholar and statesman, on the free development of each person. Retractation is withdrawing from a promise; to alienate is to give away.
readings.contentNote: Mill discusses whether either partner should be free to end a marriage and what parents owe their children; some students will have family experience of divorce.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, “Applications,” the paragraph beginning “It was pointed out in an early part of this Essay”; opens “It was pointed out in an early part of this Essay, that the liberty of the individual, in…”; closes “…as if the interest of children was everything, and that of grown persons nothing.”.

questions.prompt: Why should a contract to sell oneself as a slave be void, when Mill otherwise lets people do as they like with their own lives?
facilitatorNotes: Freedom is respected because a voluntary choice is evidence that the choice suits the chooser. Selling oneself gives up all future choices, so it defeats the very purpose that justifies the freedom; nothing shows that the slave stays willingly. Hence the paradox: freedom cannot include freedom not to be free.
evidence: His voluntary choice is evidence that what he so chooses is desirable, or at the least endurable, to him,
The principle of freedom cannot require that he should be free not to be free.
It is not freedom, to be allowed to alienate his freedom.

questions.prompt: Mill says the same reasons have “far wider application” but are limited by “the necessities of life.” Which agreements might they reach, and where must they stop?
facilitatorNotes: Any engagement that binds a person’s future self: long service contracts, perhaps some promises. But ordinary life requires accepting limits, such as a job or a lease. Mill’s proposal is that the parties may release one another, and that only contracts about money must be kept without exception. Students can test long apprenticeships, enlistment or subscription contracts.
evidence: yet a limit is everywhere set to them by the necessities of life,
except those that relate to money or money’s worth,

questions.prompt: How does Mill qualify Humboldt’s view that either partner should be able to end a marriage at will? What obligations does he say arise when people rely on us?
facilitatorNotes: When one person encourages another to build plans on his continuing conduct, new moral obligations arise; and a relationship that brings others into existence creates duties to them. These do not require keeping the contract at any cost to the unhappy party, and may not change the legal freedom much, but they change the moral freedom a great deal.
evidence: a new series of moral obligations arises on his part towards that person, which may possibly be overruled, but cannot be ignored.
has even called third parties into existence,
they necessarily make a great difference in the moral freedom.

questions.prompt: Mill ends by complaining that the question is usually discussed “as if the interest of children was everything, and that of grown persons nothing.” Given his distinction between legal and moral freedom, what balance does he want? Do you agree?
facilitatorNotes: Adults should keep the legal freedom to release themselves, but are morally bound to weigh everyone affected and are responsible if they do not. Some find this a sensible division between law and conscience; others think that moral duties without legal support leave children poorly protected, or that Mill undervalues their claims.
evidence: A person is bound to take all these circumstances into account,
as if the interest of children was everything, and that of grown persons nothing.
